why: Both content compilers append the frontmatter/meta/headings/contentFormat exports only when the author did not write them. Deciding that needs an answer to 'does this module already export NAME', and both halves answered it with a private tokenizer that knew line comments, block comments and the three quote characters but had no regular-expression branch. A regex containing a quote therefore opened a string skip that ran to the next quote anywhere in the file, so the author's own export stopped being seen as code and the generated one was appended beside it: 'Identifier already declared'. The cases below pin the decision to the one scanner per language, in both directions.
declarationCounting: 'declarations' counts occurrences of the literal substring 'export const NAME' in the compiled module, the passed-through source included. A case whose own source spells the phrase therefore expects two.

cases.name: regex holding a single quote above an authored frontmatter
cases.why: The reported reproduction. The quote inside the character class must not open a string, and the author's frontmatter must remain the only declaration.

cases.name: regex holding a double quote above an authored frontmatter
cases.why: The same blindness with the other ASCII quote, which the tokenizer also treated as a string opener.

cases.name: regex holding a backtick above an authored frontmatter
cases.why: A backtick in a character class opened a template literal that ran to end of file, so nothing after the regex was code at all.

cases.name: an export written inside template text is not an export
cases.why: Template text is not code, so the generated frontmatter is still appended and the phrase appears twice: once as the string the author wrote, once as the declaration. This is the direction the shared scanner makes stricter, and it is the intended one.
cases.source:
export const sample = `export const frontmatter = 1`

# Heading

cases.name: a backtick inside a template interpolation closes nothing
cases.why: A quoted backtick inside a ${...} ended the template early for the tokenizer, which then read the rest of the module as string content. Interpolations are code for the shared scanner.

cases.name: a re-export clause already publishes the name
cases.why: ast::has_named_runtime_export deliberately ignores re-export forms because they are a graph edge it cannot prove. The generator needs the wider answer: a clause that already binds the name makes an appended declaration a duplicate the module cannot parse.
cases.source:
export { title as frontmatter, title as meta } from './linked.js'

# Heading

cases.name: a local export clause already publishes the name
cases.why: The clause form without a `from` has to be recognised too, and the exported name is the one after `as`.

cases.name: a generator declaration already publishes the name
cases.why: `export function* frontmatter` puts the star between the keyword and the name, so a prefix list of `function `/`const `/... cannot reach past it and the export went unseen on the Rust side.

cases.name: a combining-mark identifier is one identifier
cases.why: The Rust tokenizer classified identifier characters with char::is_alphanumeric, which is false for the combining marks Thai, Devanagari, Arabic, Hebrew and Vietnamese are written with, so it split one identifier into three tokens.

cases.name: a declared name that only starts with the generated name is a different name
cases.why: `frontmatterค่า` is not `frontmatter`. An identifier-boundary check written in ASCII bytes ends the name at the combining mark and suppresses the generated export, which loses the frontmatter and the headings silently — the reverse direction of the same defect.

cases.name: a clause name that only starts with the generated name is a different name
cases.why: The same boundary question inside a clause: `{ value as frontmatterค่า }` publishes `frontmatterค่า`, so the generated frontmatter is still required.
cases.source:
export { value as frontmatterค่า } from './linked.js'

# Heading
